title: Series and parallel circuits — how components are connected matters
examTip: Both circuit types appear in every paper. Expect 'state the rule', calculation and 'explain why' questions. Two favourites keep coming back. One is the parallel resistance formula (1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2). The other is why household circuits are wired in parallel.
introTips: This covers the rules for current, voltage and resistance in series and parallel circuits
You will work through calculations for both circuit types, including the parallel resistance formula
By the end, you will be able to set up and read circuit diagrams. You will also be able to explain why real circuits are wired the way they are
intro: Components can be joined in a single loop or in separate branches. That choice completely changes how a circuit behaves. Get it wrong in a circuit diagram and everything after it is wrong. Series and parallel rules come up in calculations and in 'explain' questions. They also explain everyday things. For example, one blown bulb used to knock out a whole string of Christmas lights. Knowing both types gives you the tools to work out any circuit you are given.

keyPoints.heading: Series circuits — one loop, shared everything
keyPoints.content: In a series circuit, components are joined in a single continuous loop with no branches. So there is only one path for charge to flow. This leads to three key rules. First, current is the same everywhere in the circuit. If 2 A flows through one component, 2 A flows through all of them. Second, the potential differences add up to the supply voltage. Say a battery gives 12 V and one resistor has 8 V across it. Then the other has 4 V. Third, the total resistance is the sum of all individual resistances: Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3 + ... For example, two resistors of 3 Ω and 5 Ω in series give a total resistance of 3 + 5 = 8 Ω. Adding more components to a series circuit always increases the total resistance. So it reduces the current from the supply.
writeBullets: Series circuit — a single loop with no branches. Only one path for current
Current — the same at every point in a series circuit
Potential difference — the p.d.s across each component add up to the supply voltage
Total resistance — Rtotal = R1 + R2 + R3 (resistances add up in series)
Adding components — increases the total resistance, so the current from the supply falls
Consequence — if one component breaks in series, the circuit is broken and all components stop

keyTerms.def: Components connected in a single loop with no branches; current has only one path
Sum of individual resistances: Rtotal = R1 + R2 + ...

keyPoints.memTip: Series = Same current. 'S for Same, S for Series.' Voltages split, and resistances add.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Examiners love giving you the supply voltage and the p.d. across one component. Then they ask for the p.d. across the other. Remember: the p.d.s must add up to the supply.

keyPoints.heading: Parallel circuits — branches give choice
keyPoints.content: In a parallel circuit, components are joined in separate branches between the same two points. Charge can take different routes. This leads to three rules that are very different from series. First, the potential difference is the same across every branch, and equals the supply voltage. This is because each branch connects the same two points. Second, the current splits between branches. The branch with lower resistance carries more current. The total current from the supply equals the sum of the branch currents. Third, the total resistance is less than the smallest individual resistance. Adding branches gives charge more routes, so it flows more easily overall. The formula is 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Example: two resistors of 4 Ω and 4 Ω in parallel give 1/Rtotal = 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/4 = 0.5. So Rtotal = 2 Ω. That is exactly half of either single resistance.
writeBullets: Parallel circuit — components in separate branches. Many paths for current
Potential difference — the same across every parallel branch (equals the supply voltage)
Current — splits between branches. More current goes through the branch with lower resistance
Total current — sum of all branch currents
Total resistance — less than the smallest individual resistance
Formula — 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Take the reciprocal of the answer to get Rtotal

keyTerms.def: Components in separate branches between the same two points; voltage is equal across each branch
Found using 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2; always less than the smallest resistance

keyPoints.memTip: Parallel = same Pressure (voltage). Current splits like traffic at a junction. 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Don't forget to flip the answer at the end.
keyPoints.tutor_note: The most common mistake with the parallel resistance formula is not taking the reciprocal at the end. If you get 1/Rtotal = 0.5, then Rtotal = 1/0.5 = 2 Ω, not 0.5 Ω.

keyPoints.heading: Real-world circuits — why the wiring matters
keyPoints.content: Series and parallel help explain everyday electrical systems. Old-style Christmas tree lights were wired in series. When one bulb blew, the circuit broke and the whole string went out. Modern sets wire bulbs in parallel, so each has its own branch. Then one failure doesn't affect the others. Household mains wiring is always parallel. Each socket and appliance is on a separate branch, connected directly to the 230 V supply. This gives three benefits: - every device gets the full supply voltage (needed for devices designed for 230 V) - each can be switched on and off on its own - a fault in one appliance doesn't cut power to everything else If household circuits were in series, switching off your phone charger would turn off everything else too. That would clearly not work.
writeBullets: Christmas lights (series) — one bulb blows → the circuit breaks → they all go out
Modern lights (parallel) — one bulb blows → the other branches are not affected
Household circuits — always parallel. Each device is on its own branch
Full voltage — with parallel wiring, every appliance gets the full 230 V supply
Separate switching — each branch can be controlled on its own
Fault isolation — a fault in one appliance doesn't cut power to the whole circuit

keyTerms.def: Mains circuits wired so every appliance gets full supply voltage and can be switched independently

keyPoints.memTip: House = Parallel. Phone charger off, lights still on. That is parallel in action.
keyPoints.tutor_note: In 'explain why' questions about household wiring, you need TWO separate points. Give full voltage to each device AND separate switching. One alone is unlikely to earn full marks.

keyPoints.heading: Calculating values in mixed circuits
keyPoints.content: Many questions use circuits with both series and parallel sections. The key is to work in stages. Step 1: Replace any parallel combination with its equivalent resistance, using 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Step 2: Add any series resistors to find the overall total resistance. Step 3: Use Rtotal and the supply voltage to find the total current (I = V/R). Step 4: Work back through the circuit to find voltages and currents in each branch. Worked example: R1 = 6 Ω is in parallel with R2 = 3 Ω. These are in series with R3 = 2 Ω. Supply = 12 V. Step 1: 1/Rparallel = 1/6 + 1/3 = 1/6 + 2/6 = 3/6 = 0.5, so Rparallel = 2 Ω. Step 2: Rtotal = 2 + 2 = 4 Ω. Step 3: Itotal = 12/4 = 3 A. Step 4: V across parallel section = 3 A × 2 Ω = 6 V. V across R3 = 3 A × 2 Ω = 6 V. Check: 6 + 6 = 12 V.
writeBullets: Step 1 — find the equivalent resistance of any parallel combination first
Step 2 — add series resistors to get the overall total resistance
Step 3 — use I = V/Rtotal to find the total current from the supply
Step 4 — use V = IR in each section to find each voltage and current
Check — voltages across series sections should add up to the supply voltage
Parallel branch current — use I = V/R with the branch voltage and the branch resistance. The voltage is the same for all branches

keyTerms.def: A single resistance value that has the same effect on the circuit as a combination of resistors

keyPoints.memTip: Mixed circuits: parallel first, then add series, then I = V/R, then work back. Cover your notes and write the four steps from memory. Then try the worked example without looking.
keyPoints.tutor_note: Always check your answer at the end. The p.d.s across each series section should add up to the supply voltage. This takes 10 seconds. It catches arithmetic slips before they cost you marks.

keyPoints.heading: Measuring circuits — ammeters and voltmeters
keyPoints.content: To measure current, use an ammeter connected in series with the component. Then all the current you want to measure flows through the meter. An ammeter must have very low resistance, so it doesn't noticeably change the current in the circuit. To measure potential difference, use a voltmeter connected in parallel across the component. This puts it between the same two points as the component, so it measures the same p.d. A voltmeter must have very high resistance. Then almost no current goes through it. Any current through it would change the reading and upset the circuit. Common circuit diagram mistakes: - drawing the ammeter in parallel (it would short-circuit the component) - drawing the voltmeter in series (its high resistance would block nearly all the current) - putting meters in the wrong branch of a parallel circuit
writeBullets: Ammeter — in series with the component. Measures the current through it
Ammeter resistance — very low, so it doesn't reduce the current it is measuring
Voltmeter — in parallel with the component. Measures the p.d. across it
Voltmeter resistance — very high, so it doesn't draw current away from the circuit
Wrong ammeter position — in parallel, it short-circuits the component and gives a wrong reading
Wrong voltmeter position — in series, its high resistance blocks current and gives a wrong reading

keyTerms.def: Measures current; connected in series; has very low resistance
Measures p.d.; connected in parallel; has very high resistance

keyPoints.memTip: A for Ammeter = A for Along (in series, along the wire). V for Voltmeter = V shape (in parallel, spanning across).
keyPoints.tutor_note: Why ammeters have low resistance and voltmeters high resistance is a frequent exam question. Just saying where they go is not enough. Ammeter: low resistance, so it doesn't reduce the circuit current. Voltmeter: high resistance, so it doesn't pull current away.

tables.title: Series vs parallel circuits — key comparison
rows: Same at every point in the circuit
Splits between branches; total = sum of branch currents
Shared — adds up to supply voltage across components
Same across every branch — equals supply voltage
Sum of all resistances: Rtotal = R1 + R2 + ...
Total resistance decreases; current from supply increases
Circuit breaks — all components stop working
Other branches continue to work independently
Household mains wiring, modern Christmas lights

0.question: Two resistors of 6 Ω and 10 Ω are connected in series with a 16 V supply. What is the current in the circuit?
0.correctFeedback: Correct. Rtotal = 6 + 10 = 16 Ω; I = V/R = 16/16 = 1 A. A textbook series circuit calculation.
0.wrongFeedback: Step 1: add the resistances. Rtotal = 6 + 10 = 16 Ω. Step 2: use I = V/R = 16 ÷ 16 = 1 A. Remember, in series you always add the resistances before using I = V/R.

1.question: Two resistors of 4 Ω and 12 Ω are connected in parallel. What is the total resistance of this combination?
1.correctFeedback: Correct. 1/Rtotal = 1/4 + 1/12 = 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12 = 1/3, so Rtotal = 3 Ω. Notice it is less than the smaller resistor (4 Ω), as it should be in parallel.
1.wrongFeedback: Use 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2 = 1/4 + 1/12. Use a common denominator: 3/12 + 1/12 = 4/12. So 1/Rtotal = 4/12, which means Rtotal = 12/4 = 3 Ω. The most common mistake is not flipping at the end, leaving 4/12 instead of 3 Ω.

3.question: In a parallel circuit, the supply voltage is 9 V. What is the potential difference across each branch?
options: It depends on the number of branches
3 V per branch if there are 3 branches
Less than 9 V because branches share the voltage
3.correctFeedback: Exactly right. In a parallel circuit, every branch connects the same two points. So every branch has the full supply voltage across it. This is one of the basic parallel rules.
3.wrongFeedback: In a parallel circuit, voltage does NOT split between branches. That happens in series. Every parallel branch connects directly between the same two points as the supply. So each branch has the full 9 V across it. Current splits; voltage doesn't.

commonMistakes: Using series voltage rules for parallel circuits. In parallel, every branch has the FULL supply voltage, not a share of it.
Not taking the reciprocal at the end of the parallel resistance formula. If 1/Rtotal = 0.25, then Rtotal = 4 Ω, not 0.25 Ω.
Thinking total parallel resistance is the average of the single resistances. It is always less than the smallest one.
Putting the ammeter in parallel instead of in series. This short-circuits the component and gives a meaningless reading.
Not checking that series voltages add up to the supply voltage. This quick check catches arithmetic slips that would lose calculation marks.
examTips: For any series circuit calculation, always find Rtotal first by adding all the resistances. Then use I = V/Rtotal to get the current. Remember, the current is the same everywhere.
For parallel resistance, write out 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2. Work out the right-hand side, then flip it to get Rtotal. Showing each step earns method marks.
When explaining why household circuits are parallel, give two points. (1) Each device gets the full supply voltage. (2) Devices can be switched on and off separately.
In mixed circuit questions, label your working clearly. For example: 'parallel combination = X Ω, then total = X + Y = Z Ω'. This makes it easy for the examiner to give partial credit.
Always check that your final answer makes physical sense. Parallel resistance must be less than the smallest branch resistance. Adding a series resistor must increase the total resistance.
revisionCardBullets: Series: current the same everywhere. Voltages add up to the supply. Rtotal = R1 + R2
Parallel: voltage the same across all branches (= supply). Current splits. 1/Rtotal = 1/R1 + 1/R2
Parallel total resistance is always less than the smallest individual resistance
Series — one component breaks: the whole circuit fails
Parallel — one branch breaks: the other branches keep working
Household wiring is parallel: full voltage to each device, and separate switching
Ammeter — in series, with very low resistance
Voltmeter — in parallel, with very high resistance
Mixed circuits: find parallel equivalent first, then add series resistors
Use I = V/R after finding Rtotal to get total current from supply
Check series answers: the p.d.s across all sections must add up to the supply voltage
Current in a parallel branch: I = Vbranch / Rbranch. The voltage is the same for all branches
